One bounded cross-examination completed: inspected the opposite EUGN frozen review and incoming two-check package, resolved against the already-read manuscript. No additional personas, external sources, or historical outcomes were consulted.
score_reason: 5: Marginally below acceptance threshold. The static-memory supervised retrieval construction is coherent: gradients are taken through the selected-set loss, not established through approximate or sampled retrieval itself. The exact-MIPS comparison gives a useful accuracy gain in the reported QA setting with similar epoch-wise convergence. However, scalable training is the main contribution, and candidate-access counts at one approximately 108k-fact scale do not establish measured end-to-end costs. Following cross-examination, I explicitly do not require parity with full-softmax accuracy: a lower-accuracy operating point could be useful under a demonstrated resource budget. The missing evidence is a measured, useful cost-accuracy frontier or compelling budgeted operating point, not proof that all quality loss can be eliminated. Unestablished bias-reduction explanations and incomplete retrieval settings and variability reporting further limit reliability. No fatal defect in the core algorithm has been demonstrated.
change_reason: Score remains 5. Cross-examination confirmed the bounded trainability strength and the factual speed-evidence gap. I clarified that gradients through the conditional selected-set objective do not establish differentiability of retrieval, and narrowed the utility framing so equality with full-softmax accuracy is not required. These clarifications do not supply the missing measured efficiency or reproducibility evidence that determines my assessment.

evidence.claim: The proposed learning construction is coherent under the explicitly fixed-memory, gold-fact-supervised conditions.
evidence.location: Sections 2-3, especially p.4 Equations (2)-(4), gold-candidate insertion, and the paragraph fixing memory representations; Section 5.2.
evidence.observation: The reader retrieves a candidate subset, normalizes scores over that subset, and backpropagates the correct-fact loss while the memory vectors stay fixed. Inserting the gold fact avoids an undefined training target when initial retrieval misses it. For a fixed selected subset this is an ordinary differentiable classification loss; exact top-K selection is locally unchanged away from score ties. The paper explicitly separates exact selection from approximate retrieval and does not conceal the fully supervised setting.
evidence.consequence: This supplies a plausible and implementable route for learning the query against a fixed external index without requiring a reinforcement-learning estimator. The construction itself does not establish equivalence to full-softmax training or apply automatically to learned writable memory.
evidence.scope: Static external facts with labeled supporting facts; the conclusion concerns well-defined training, not global convergence or universal memory architectures.
evidence.would_change_judgment: This is a central positive consideration; evidence that gold insertion was incorrectly used at test time or that the stated loss was not implemented would substantially weaken it, but neither is established by the manuscript.

evidence.claim: Exact-MIPS training yields a useful controlled empirical gain within the reported simplified QA model.
evidence.location: Sections 5.2-5.4; Table 1 and Figure 1 on p.8.
evidence.observation: With the stated fixed TransE memory and learned question embeddings, Table 1 reports 62.2% for 10-MIPS against 59.5% for full softmax, with intermediate K values yielding intermediate accuracies. The actual training candidate sizes are disclosed: 1,290 for 10-MIPS versus 108,442 for full softmax, because candidates are shared across the minibatch. Figure 1 shows similar epoch-wise convergence rather than a severe optimization delay.
evidence.consequence: The observation supports studying selected high-score negatives as a useful training intervention, rather than treating retrieval solely as a test-time shortcut. It supports the narrower empirical gain without proving the proposed gradient explanation.
evidence.scope: The reported single dataset and architecture, exact retrieval, and the stated minibatch-union protocol; no wall-clock gain follows for exact MIPS.
evidence.would_change_judgment: Replication of this gain with uncertainty estimates and matched candidate-set controls would increase confidence; the reported result already contributes positively.

evidence.claim: The central training-speed and scalability claim is not established by the reported cost evidence.
evidence.location: Introduction contribution bullets on p.3; Section 3.1 on p.5; Section 5.5 on p.8; Table 2 on p.9.
evidence.observation: Section 3.1 says a read requires only K centroid dot products, but the selected fact scores and softmax in Equation (4) must also be computed. Section 5.5 infers a 5X speedup from approximately 20,000 fact accesses versus 108,442; it provides no measured end-to-end timing, hardware, index construction cost, or scaling curve. Table 2 shows convergence ranging from 16 to 68 epochs, so a similar per-query access budget does not establish similar total training cost. The best approximate result is 53.1%, below full softmax's 59.5%, and no time-to-common-accuracy comparison is provided.
evidence.consequence: Reduced candidate scoring is credible, but the size of a real training speedup, its overheads, and its usefulness at comparable predictive quality remain unresolved. This directly limits the stated primary motivation.
evidence.scope: The manuscript's reported scalability evidence; this does not assert that approximate retrieval cannot be faster.
evidence.remedy: Report preprocessing and per-epoch training/inference wall time on stated hardware, total time to convergence, and an accuracy-cost curve across memory sizes. Count both centroid search and selected-fact scoring; explicitly label access-count ratios as such.
evidence.would_change_judgment: Yes. A convincing measured accuracy-versus-time improvement and scaling trend would materially raise the score.

evidence.claim: The claim that the proposed additions decrease gradient bias is stronger than the argument and ablations establish.
evidence.location: Section 3 p.4 gradient explanation; Section 3.1 p.5 candidate-union and sampling bullets; Section 5.5 and Table 2.
evidence.observation: For the Section 5.2 loss, the full-softmax query gradient is the probability-weighted mean of all memory vectors minus the gold vector; the subset loss replaces that mean with a renormalized mean over selected candidates. Candidate union or extra sampling changes this surrogate, but the paper supplies neither a defined bias measure nor a derivation or measurement showing monotone reduction in gradient error. Table 2 measures final accuracy and epochs: it supports a beneficial sampling heuristic in several configurations, not an identified reduction in gradient bias.
evidence.consequence: The algorithm remains usable, but the mechanistic account is not established. In particular, improved accuracy cannot by itself show that the full-softmax gradient is better approximated, especially when exact truncation already outperforms full softmax.
evidence.scope: The explanatory statements about gradient bias, not the correctness of using a truncated objective or a requirement for a general convergence theorem.
evidence.remedy: Define the target gradient and compare gradient discrepancy or omitted probability mass in this manageable setting, or present bias reduction as a hypothesis and describe the methods as candidate-coverage heuristics.
evidence.would_change_judgment: Clarifying this would strengthen the insight contribution; it would not by itself resolve the missing scalability evidence.

evidence.claim: Important settings and reliability checks are missing for reproducing and interpreting the approximate-retrieval comparison.
evidence.observation: The paper states the optimizer, learning rate, batch size, fact dimensionality, early stopping, and cluster counts, but does not report the selected augmentation parameters U and m, numbers of top and sampled clusters, random-block size, or the final WTA/PCA configurations used to achieve comparable access budgets. No seed counts or variability estimates accompany differences such as 52.8 versus 53.1. Gold-fact retrieval recall is also absent, so Table 1's approximation losses cannot be separated into candidate exclusion and learned scoring errors.
evidence.consequence: The large clustering-versus-tree/hash difference is suggestive, but the precise matched-cost setup and smaller strategy ranking are difficult to audit or reproduce. The source of the approximate model's substantial loss remains uncertain.
evidence.scope: Reporting and reliability of the tested settings; no claim is made that uninspected code or raw results do not exist.
evidence.remedy: Give a complete hyperparameter table and selection protocol, replicate the key configurations, and report gold-fact retrieval recall separately from accuracy conditional on retrieval.
evidence.would_change_judgment: Yes, jointly with measured costs. Stable results under documented matched-cost settings would make the empirical contribution substantially more dependable.

evidence.claim: Several general conclusions exceed the tested conditions, despite the paper's useful explicit restrictions.
evidence.location: Section 5.1 p.6; Section 5.4 p.7; related-work discussion of SAM on p.6; conclusion p.9.
evidence.observation: The experiments deliberately use only the SimpleQuestions fact collection rather than the cited 10M/12M fact memories, and train only bag-of-words question embeddings against fixed fact representations. Nevertheless, Section 5.4 recommends a K-MIPS layer instead of softmax whenever possible, and the related-work discussion extrapolates clustering improvements to SAM despite a different writable-memory setting. No hard-attention baseline, changing-memory experiment, or larger-memory study supports those extensions.
evidence.consequence: The evidence supports a promising static supervised-QA case study, not broad superiority over soft attention, demonstrated ease versus hard attention, or transfer to controller-written memory. Those wider conclusions increase the apparent significance beyond what has been established.
evidence.scope: Breadth of claims relative to supplied experiments. The limited test scope is not itself a demand for state-of-the-art QA or modern baselines.
evidence.remedy: Qualify the general recommendations as hypotheses, retain the stated static-memory boundary, and use any added experiment to test the specific broader claim being retained.
evidence.would_change_judgment: Claim narrowing improves accuracy of presentation; evidence at a materially larger memory size would also address the central score-limiting issue.

challenges.challenge: Confirmed for the disclosed static, gold-fact-supervised setting: p.4 Equations (3)–(4) define candidate-restricted normalization, the next paragraphs insert the correct training fact and freeze memory, and Section 5.2 p.7 specifies the correct-fact NLL. The exact top-K loss is locally differentiable away from selection changes, and Table 1/Figure 1 p.8 provide empirical feasibility evidence beyond that mathematical coherence. Please retain the distinction between differentiating the conditional selected-set loss and differentiating the approximate or sampled retrieval procedure itself; neither the text nor these experiments establishes the latter. The strongest positive I infer is a trainable query-to-fixed-index interface, with a measured exact-selection accuracy gain, rather than a generally differentiable memory-access mechanism.
challenges.response: Agreed. The positive claim in dicr-e1 is specifically mathematical coherence and trainability for a fixed selected set, with local constancy of exact top-K away from ties. It does not claim differentiability through approximate index routing, sampled cluster choice, or selection boundaries. Equations (3)-(4) on p.4 and the Section 5.2 NLL on p.7 support differentiating the conditional selected-set objective with respect to query embeddings. Table 1/Figure 1 on p.8 separately provide empirical feasibility for the exact-selection training protocol. I retain that bounded positive assessment: learning a query against a fixed index, not a generally differentiable retrieval mechanism.

challenges.challenge: The factual objection is sound: Section 5.5 p.8 ties 5X to approximately 20,000 fact accesses, Table 2 p.9 reports substantially differing epoch counts, and Equation (4) p.4 requires scoring selected facts in addition to the centroid computations mentioned on p.5. These do not establish wall-clock acceleration. I would qualify any implication that comparable predictive quality is required before the contribution can have utility: the stated experimental aim on p.6 is a speed–accuracy tradeoff, and a lower-accuracy operating point could be useful if actual savings and an application-relevant budget were demonstrated. Can the decisive missing evidence be framed as a measured, useful cost–accuracy frontier rather than mandatory equality with full-softmax accuracy? This preserves the major speed-evidence criticism while distinguishing an unresolved tradeoff from a demonstrated lack of utility.
challenges.response: Agreed on the distinction. My reference to comparable predictive quality in dicr-e3 is a useful diagnostic, not a mandatory acceptance criterion or a claim that lower-accuracy retrieval has no utility. Section 5 on p.6 explicitly studies speed-accuracy tradeoffs. A demonstrated lower-accuracy operating point could be worthwhile under a real resource budget. The decisive deficit is therefore the absence of measured end-to-end costs establishing a useful cost-accuracy frontier or even a compelling budgeted operating point. Table 2 epoch counts and the selected-fact scoring required by Equation (4) prevent translating the access ratio directly into such evidence. I narrow the utility framing accordingly while retaining the major unsupported-speed objection.
